chapter_title: Concerning why if a [Nail] is cut the Person shall not be sick; but if a Limb is cut he shall immediately be pained.
chapter_note: Heavily lacunose chapter preserving a body-cosmos correspondence teaching: body↔earth, limbs↔trees, varieties of trees↔varieties of body parts (some regrow when cut, others do not). This is systematic body-cosmos mapping consistent with the substrate pattern identified in Ch.70. The teaching purity score of 0.0 is misleading — the substrate vocabulary here uses common terms (body, earth, trees) rather than the marked zoomorphic/metal terms the pipeline detects. The STRUCTURE is pure correspondential mapping: both sides stay within the natural/cosmic system. Dialogue frame is dominant by paragraph count (5 of 7) but the two teaching paragraphs contain the bulk of the word count. No editorial bridge, institutional, or exhortation layers detected — this chapter appears to be substrate teaching wrapped in dialogue frame with no later editorial extension.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Standard dialogue frame formula: 'Once again one of the disciples questioned the apostle. He says to him:' — purely formulaic with no cosmological content.

paragraphs.core_text: why when limbs are cut from the body of the person he shall be pained? While if the hair on the head of the person's body should be shaved, and [the nai]ls o]f his hands and feet be cut, he does not notice it [...] Some of these even now shall grow an[d ...] again. Just as the na[ils ...] so the hair shall grow and [...] cut a finger, he in [...] on the limbs of the [bod]y that you [.. ⟨p.281⟩ ...] him [...] since this time to the [... ...] the body ag[a]in.
paragraphs.removed_material: Removed 'Tell me, my master,' — dialogue frame address formula wrapping the substantive question.
paragraphs.temporal_note: The question defines the teaching structure: it identifies the phenomenon (differential pain and regrowth in body parts) that the body-cosmos correspondence will explain. The observation itself — that nails/hair regrow when cut but fingers/limbs do not — is the empirical basis for the tree-variety mapping in ¶5. This is a substantive cosmological question in the Persian pedagogical tradition. Very fragmentary in the second half.
Pure plea formula: 'I beseech you, my master, that you might instruct me' — no cosmological content, only honorific address requesting instruction.
Pure dialogue attribution: 'Then the a[postle] speaks to him:' — standard response-introduction formula.

paragraphs.temporal_note: Core body-cosmos correspondence: body↔earth, limbs↔trees. The teaching then classifies tree varieties by regrowth behavior — some grow back when cut, others do not — and maps these back to body parts. Both sides of the mapping stay within the natural/cosmic system. This is the same body-cosmos correspondence tradition attested in Ch.70. Despite heavy lacunae, the structure is clear: systematic classification of body-part types through tree-variety analogy. The final lines about 'impurity' and 'flesh that is corrupt' / 'living flesh' suggest the teaching also addressed the mixture of living and dead substance in the body — a substrate concern.
Formulaic closure: 'Behold, I have taught you about this lesson for which you have asked me' — standard dialogue-frame conclusion wrapping the teaching unit.
Narrative closure: 'the disciple heard this homily... he sat down' — standard session-ending formula. Very fragmentary.
